name: Blood doping

lead: Blood doping increases the number of red blood cells so the blood carries more oxygen to working muscles. That raises aerobic capacity, which athletes use to train and compete at higher endurance output.

Its connection to looks is indirect: the aerobic work it supports is associated with leanness and conditioning, but it is a sport-performance practice and is banned in competition. Research has established the physiology well, and anti-doping science has developed detection methods.

paras: Described methods include transfusing stored blood, drugs such as erythropoietin (EPO) that stimulate red cell production, and substances that mimic low oxygen such as cobalt. These are covered here as history and science, not as instructions.

Thicker blood can reduce flow and raise risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism, and transfusions carry infection and contamination risks. Cobalt has documented toxicity. The practice is prohibited by anti-doping rules and monitored via blood testing.

chain: More red blood cells and hemoglobin
Greater oxygen delivery and aerobic capacity
Supports more or harder aerobic training
angle.text: The practice aims at aerobic performance. Its link to physique is only through the training capacity it permits; it is prohibited in sport and carries severe risks.

lead: Blood doping is the use of transfusion, erythropoietin or related substances to raise red blood cell mass so the blood carries more oxygen. It is mainly an endurance-sport practice; any link to appearance runs through the training volume and conditioning it is meant to support.

Physiology research shows maximal oxygen uptake is limited by oxygen delivery, and that blood doping changes it accordingly [1]. A review of blood volume adaptations notes that blood doping mimics altitude effects but far exceeds their magnitude [2].

Blood doping has a long history in sport, with documented cases in cycling, athletics and mountaineering-style endurance events, and it has been banned by the International Olympic Committee since the mid-1980s [3]. Detection now relies on flow cytometry for transfusions from another person and monitoring of blood values over time, including the athlete biological passport [3][4].

paras: Wikipedia describes blood doping as increasing red cell number to improve aerobic capacity and endurance, using drugs, transfusions or blood substitutes [3]. EPO, a kidney hormone first developed for patients undergoing chemotherapy, was later misused by cyclists [3].

In 1947 US military researchers transfused red cells into ten men to raise tolerance to altitude [3]. Blood doping reached sport in the late 1960s among distance runners [3]. Finnish runner Kaarlo Maaninka was transfused before winning medals at the 1980 Moscow Olympics, when it was not against the rules [3]. The IOC banned the practice in the mid-1980s, and a flow cytometry test for transfusion from another person arrived in 2004 [3]. Lance Armstrong was stripped of seven Tour de France titles in 2012 and admitted transfusion and EPO use in 2013 [3].

Training raises blood volume through plasma and red cell expansion, whereas hypoxia raises red cell volume only, and blood doping exceeds altitude's effect [2]. A 1987 controlled trial examined reinfusion of autologous blood on exercise performance in cross-country skiers [5]. Cobalt stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor and so stimulates EPO production [6].

Increased blood viscosity can reduce flow and cardiac output, and excess EPO raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism [3]. Contamination during storage can cause sepsis [3]. Cobalt toxicity has been reviewed in the literature [6]. Hemoglobin-based blood substitutes were halted in trials because of increased death and heart attack risk [3].

Flow cytometry detects mixed blood populations from another person, and CO rebreathing measures total hemoglobin mass for autologous transfusions [3]. Reviews describe the haematological module of the athlete biological passport and earlier feasibility work [4][7].

Human trials include a controlled study of autologous blood reinfusion in skiers [5] and randomised trials developing biomarkers, such as erythroferrone, to detect stimulated red cell production [8]. No studies were identified testing blood doping for appearance outcomes.
